title: Where Should Humans Stay in the Loop? A Five-Stage Framework for AI-Assisted Social Science
text: Large language models are rapidly becoming part of the social scientist's methodological toolkit. Researchers now use them to annotate political texts, generate experimental stimuli, simulate respondents, discover patterns in large corpora, write code, and even reproduce published studies. The usual debate asks a simple question: **How much should researchers rely on AI?** I think that is the wrong question. AI does not play the same epistemic role at every stage of research. A model that is useful for brainstorming a possible explanation may be wholly inappropriate for validating a measurement. title: Five Common Pitfalls in Hypothesis Building
text: A hypothesis is more than a statement that two variables are related. A useful hypothesis should represent a theoretically meaningful claim that could, at least in principle, be shown to be wrong. This sounds straightforward, but many hypotheses that appear reasonable at first glance contain hidden problems. Some are true simply because of the way the concepts are defined. Others reason backward from an observed outcome, mix different levels of analysis, reduce complex social phenomena to a single level of explanation, or interpret correlation as evidence of causation. title: AI as Emerging Institutional Power in Journalism
text: Artificial intelligence is increasingly discussed in journalism as a new tool: something journalists use to write, summarize, translate, analyze data, personalize content, or automate routine work. Much of the debate therefore revolves around questions of use and effects. How effectively can journalists work with AI? How do audiences respond to AI-generated news? What policies should news organizations adopt? These are important questions, but they may begin too far downstream. A more fundamental question is what happens when journalism becomes dependent on technological systems whose infrastructures, rules, values, and conditions of access are largely determined outside journalism itself. title: Word2Vec: Learning Word Meaning from Context
text: Word2Vec is a neural embedding framework designed to learn dense, low-dimensional vector representations of words from raw text. Its central idea is simple but powerful: words that appear in similar linguistic environments should be located close to one another in the embedding space. In this sense, Word2Vec operationalizes a modern version of the distributional hypothesis: a word can be understood by the company it keeps. It does so through a computationally efficient neural architecture that learns word meaning from patterns of co-occurrence. ## Two architectures: CBOW and Skip-gram There are two main variants of Word2Vec: **CBOW** and **Skip-gram**. title: Detecting Divisive Language: A Concept-Grounded NLP Pipeline
text: This note introduces an NLP pipeline I developed with collaborators for detecting divisive language in polarized social media discourse. The paper was published in the **Proceedings of the Twentieth International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2026)**. title: Calling Perspective API in Python
text: Perspective API is a machine-learning-based tool that scores the perceived attributes of a piece of text, such as toxicity, insult, threat, profanity, identity attack, or other forms of potentially harmful language. This note summarizes how Perspective API works conceptually and how to call it in Python for computational social science research. Download the code on GitHub ## What is Perspective API? Perspective API is a free API that uses machine learning models to score attributes of a comment or text.
